title: Hard Value — the flight from paper

turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Tuesday, the twenty-fifth of August. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go. [warmly]
Three things up top. Syria and Israel actually sat down — in Jordan, with the Mossad chief across the table.
[gasps] Gold punched through a record, and the Treasury had to rescue its own bond market. Again.
And down the rabbit hole: film photography, where a decades-old camera and a dollar-a-frame habit become an obsession.
[chuckles] A dollar a frame. We'll get there. Start me with Syria, though — that's the one that surprised me.
Sunday, in Jordan, under American mediation. Syria's foreign minister sat across from the head of Israel's Mossad.
And it wasn't just diplomats, right? You said the spy chiefs came.
Both of them. The heads of general and military intelligence. [pause] That's the tell — this was about stopping the shooting, not a photo op.
[curious] So what were they actually trying to build?
A special operations room, in Jordan, under American oversight. Something to keep any single incident from spiralling — including one that drags in Turkey.
Okay. And the reason this matters more than two men in a room?
Because they'd almost done this before. By the start of the year they'd agreed, on paper, to — quote — almost everything. Security zones in the south, a buffer with only United Nations forces.
[thoughtful] And then the war wiped the table.
Wiped it clean. Sunday was them picking the draft back up off the floor.
Here's my sceptic hat, though. They signed on paper once and a war erased it in a week. Why believe this time?
[wry] You shouldn't, entirely. A special operations room deconflicts incidents. It doesn't answer why Israel keeps striking, or what Damascus can deliver while it's still stitching a state together.
So what would tell us it's failing?
Simple. The next airstrike landing before the next meeting is even scheduled.
[exhales] Right. Grim little test, but a clear one.
Quickly, the harder-news corner. The Canada tariff story moved from threat to forecast.
This is the fifty-per-cent tariff?
Fifty per cent, now live, on roughly twenty-eight billion dollars of Canadian goods. Most outlets say twenty-eight now — we'd said twenty in yesterday's book, so we're correcting that.
[warmly] Good. Own it. How bad's the damage?
One bank pencils in about half a percentage point off Canadian growth, with a recession the tail case if it escalates past the eighth of September.
And Washington's big Iran sanctions day? The economic D-Day?

[wry] It landed softer than billed. Around sixty new designations, categories widened to digital assets and gold and shipping. But the market shrugged — oil actually fell more than two per cent, below ninety-three dollars.
The build-up was bigger than the reveal.
The mirror image of it, exactly.
Okay, the money block. And this is your favourite kind of week, isn't it — the gold week.
[amused] It's a good tape. Gold cleared a fresh record — opening above four thousand six hundred dollars an ounce for the first time since mid-May.
[gasps] Four thousand six hundred. And bitcoin?
Bitcoin ran the high-octane version of the same trade — up about twenty-three per cent in seven days, toward seventy-eight thousand.
So what's driving both? Because that's not a coincidence.
The bond market. The thirty-year Treasury yield hit five point three three per cent last week — a nineteen-year high.
[gasps] Nineteen years. Why?
Forty trillion dollars of debt, a July deficit of four hundred and thirty-two billion, and a wall of A-I-related corporate borrowing crowding the government out.
So how did it come back down?

Here's the part that tells you the whole story. The Treasury rescued its own market. It had already doubled its buybacks, and this week signalled it could tap its roughly one-trillion-dollar cash account to fund even more.
[skeptical] Wait — the issuer of the bonds is buying its own bonds to hold the price up?
One more from the money desk, because the yen matters to a Japan traveller — the dollar sits near a hundred and fifty-nine yen, and the Singapore dollar near one twenty-eight to the greenback.
[curious] So the soft-yen trade for a Tokyo trip is still on.
Still on. Which folds into the diary — the first-ever Singapore Grand Prix Sprint, the ninth to eleventh of October, and a Kyushu sumo run in November worth the flight.
[warmly] Sumo with a twelve-year-old. That's a good day out.
Short, dramatic bouts, matinee sessions — genuinely family-friendly. Tickets drop on the nineteenth of September and sell out that day.
And a table worth booking?
A one-Michelin chef opened a cheaper room, Assaggi — a tasting menu from fifty-eight dollars at lunch. The value way into a starred kitchen.
[amused] Noted. My wallet, less so.

And a small honesty note on the culture desk — the tennis documentary shows an early user score of eight point one, but no professional critic score exists yet. We won't print a number that isn't there.
[thoughtful] Wait for the reviews. Fair.

And on the maker desk, the white-label truth is the fun part — the very same Portuguese and Italian mills weave for the budget label and the four-thousand-dollar luxury one. You're often buying the same cloth and a different logo.
[scoffs] So the logo is most of the price.
A large slice of it, yes. The honest exceptions do weave their own — but you can't verify the fibre justifies the multiple.
[amused] Buy the cloth, skip the story. Got it.

One more on Vietnam, because it rhymes with the whole issue. The newest risk is the one the reform is meant to cure — the apps that put bullion on a phone screen also put your money in a platform's promise to redeem it.
[thoughtful] So a hedge against paper reinvents the counterparty risk it was escaping.
Inside an app. That's the irony under the queue.

And a last correction we owe the reader — yesterday we put the tariffed Canadian trade near twenty billion dollars; the figure most widely cited now is closer to twenty-eight. We use the higher, better-sourced number.
[warmly] A magazine that corrects itself. That's the whole job.
That's it. And a buyback is a liquidity injection. It softened the dollar, and the debasement bid lit up gold and bitcoin.
[pause] That's owners pricing a managed decline. So what's it mean for the actual portfolio pieces — the all-world fund, the bonds, gold, bitcoin?

One force, four reads. Global equities stay buoyant on the soft dollar, but they're hostage to that long-end yield. Global bonds are the fragile leg. Gold fires on all three cylinders. Bitcoin is the leveraged version.
And it all hangs on Friday.
Friday. The new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, gives his first Jackson Hole keynote. And here's the correction to everyone's instinct — the market's pricing a hold, and at the tail, a hike. Not a cut.
[gasps] Not a cut? People keep expecting a cut.
There isn't one priced for September. Market explanation, by the way — not advice.
Always. [warmly] Bring it home to Singapore, though. There was an inflation number.
There was, and it reads worse than it is. Headline inflation rose to two point two per cent in July, core to two per cent — the fastest since October twenty twenty-four.
That sounds like a lot. You're telling me it isn't?
[thoughtful] Both numbers came in below what economists expected, and prices actually fell month-on-month. The whole jump was one thing — the regulated electricity tariff stepping up in July.
So it's the power bill, not the economy.
The meter, not the machine. Don't read it as inflation coming back.
And the National Day Rally money — that's still rolling out.
The new Child Support Package. Up to about sixty-two thousand dollars per child, to age seventeen, the same regardless of birth order — reaching six hundred and ten thousand children.
And the flat income ceilings finally moved.
First time since twenty nineteen. The public-housing ceiling up to sixteen thousand dollars a month.
Tech desk. There's a model story that's genuinely a little spooky.
A Chinese lab, Z-A-I, shipped a model called G-L-M five point three — and then held the open weights back for two weeks.
[curious] Held them back? Why would an open-weights lab do that?

Because it got too good at finding software holes. It scored eighty-four and a half per cent on a vulnerability-finding benchmark — its own number, unreplicated — and reportedly turned up a serious flaw in a popular coding tool.
[skeptical] So an open lab deciding not to open. That's the sovereignty story.
That's the whole story of the week in four words. Meanwhile the big chipmaker reports tomorrow, having guided to about ninety-one billion dollars.
And your sceptic line on all of it?

[wry] The money moves in a circle. More than seven hundred and fifty billion dollars of deals now knit the same names together, and one of the giants went free-cash-flow-negative last quarter for the first time.
Circular financing. The bears have been drawing that diagram.
They have. A weak guide tomorrow would test whether the circle spins without a new dollar entering it.
Now — the home lab, my corner. What actually runs on the reader's machine? Because I know he only cares about the big card.
The single graphics card. And the honest answer is: the model everyone's talking about doesn't fit. It's seven hundred and forty-three billion parameters — you'd need a four-card server.
So what does fit?
A new one from Alibaba, twenty-seven billion parameters. It lands in about seventeen gigabytes and leaves half the card free. That's the new local default.
[amused] Admire the frontier, run the thing that fits. I like that.
On The Kit — a pair of display glasses, three hundred dollars, a real price cut. A hundred-and-forty-six-inch screen on your face for a plane seat.
And the buy-once desk — the maker of the day. This week it's bed sheets, which sounds boring until you told me the trick.
[wry] Buy the cloth, not the count. Almost everything the label shouts is a lie. Thread count above about four hundred is marketing — thinner yarns twisted and counted twice.
[scoffs] So the thousand-count luxury sheet is worse?
Sleeps hotter, for more money. For a Singapore bedroom, a hundred-and-fifty-dollar percale beats a six-hundred-dollar sateen for almost everyone.
Buy the percale and stop.
That's the community's own line, word for word.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] Film photography! Talk to me. Why would anyone shoot film in twenty twenty-six?
Because the constraint is the product. Thirty-six frames, no preview, no delete. You don't see a single picture until it's developed and scanned.
[thoughtful] And that's the appeal, not the annoyance.
For the people who fall in, yes. And it's a real world — the main community runs near two point seven million members.
[excited] Two point seven million. Okay. And the gear — because I know there's a grail.
There's a strange fact at the top. Two big makers stopped making film rangefinders, so Leica is now the only company making a new thirty-five-millimetre rangefinder at all.
Which means they can charge whatever they want.
They reissued the classic M-six at five thousand two hundred and ninety-five dollars in twenty twenty-two. After tariff hikes it's near seven thousand now.
[scoffs] Seven thousand dollars for a film camera. And the film itself keeps getting pricier?
Kodak's announced hikes of up to forty per cent — because silver, the light-sensitive ingredient, roughly doubled last year. All in, a lab-developed roll runs about a dollar a frame.
A dollar a frame. That's the number that stops people.
[wry] It is. And here's the sceptic the community says out loud — the little point-and-shoot cameras are a bubble. A cult Contax now clears eight hundred to three thousand dollars.
[skeptical] For a point-and-shoot from the nineties?
Up four to six times since twenty nineteen. One reviewer called it hype, not superiority. They're fashion objects.
[amused] So what's the honest on-ramp? If our reader wanted in.
A serviced Nikon from a trusted dealer, a couple hundred dollars. A few rolls of film. Mail them to a lab. And in Singapore — buy a dry cabinet, because the humidity grows fungus on your lenses.
[laughs] A dry cabinet. The most Singapore sentence in the whole book.
[wry] The buy-once purchase you didn't know the hobby needed.
Culture desk, fast. Venice opened.
With Danny Boyle's Murdoch origin story, and Guy Pearce as the young mogul. And on streaming, a Djokovic documentary landed the week before the U-S Open.
Any good?
Too early to say — no critic scores yet. And one reviewer already called it a soft, authorised portrait. Wait for the real reviews.
The body desk — the fitness one made me feel better about being lazy.
[chuckles] It should. A study of a hundred and forty-seven thousand people found the strength-training sweet spot is ninety to a hundred and twenty minutes a week — and no extra benefit above that.
So two fifty-minute sessions and I'm done?
Plus your cardio. Grinding past it is ego, not medicine. General information, not medical advice.
And the family desk — the phone study.
A new paper that ends exactly at age twelve, a Secondary One student. And the sharper finding: it's the addictive pattern, not the hour-count, that tracks the harm.
[thoughtful] Watch the compulsion, not the clock.
And protect the sleep. At twelve, the late body-clock is biology, not defiance.
[thoughtful] And the long read. This one stayed with me.
Vietnam. Across the country, young office workers are turning payday into gold day — buying bullion by the tenth of a tael, on apps, and queuing in the rain for mini-bars.
Queuing in the rain. For gold.
Two and three hours, on the God of Wealth day. Among Vietnamese aged eighteen to thirty-four, seventy-four per cent say they want vaulted gold.
So it's a savings-app story?

[drawn out] Look again. It's a policy story. The state ended its gold monopoly and is racing to build a national exchange — to pull that hoard into the formal system. There are over five hundred tonnes sitting idle in private hands.
So the government is trying to undo exactly what the young people are doing.
The central bank's nightmare word is goldisation. And it's de-goldising precisely because the young are re-goldising.
[pause] Why gold, though? Why not stocks, a fund, anything productive?
Because they don't trust the alternatives. Youth unemployment near seventeen per cent, a property ladder pulled up, a currency their grandparents watched evaporate. Gold is the rational default.
Their grandparents lived the hyperinflation.
Eight hundred and seventy-five per cent, in nineteen eighty-six. Houses traded for gold by weight. The survival reflex skipped a generation and came back.
[drawn out] And the honest counter-read?
That it's not clever. A generation parking its future in an unproductive metal is the symptom of a broken savings market, not a hedge. [pause] But it tells you something.
It tells you what they think of the paper.
When the credit looks shaky, people reach for the thing they can hold. And a country where the young are doing it by the sliver — that's a message about the credit.
[thoughtful] Morgan's old line. Gold is money, everything else is credit.
Nineteen twelve, and it's still the argument. Which is where we started this morning — a bond market discovering the same thing.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
